title: Long-term Outcomes of Prostatic Artery Embolisation: A Nationwide Prospective Cohort Study
article_subtype: Nationwide multicentre prospective cohort study with a cross-sectional long-term questionnaire component
condition_or_topic: Prostatic artery embolisation (PAE) for lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
clinical_background: LUTS can substantially reduce quality of life and affect at least 30% of men older than 65 yr. They commonly occur with BPH and may also affect men with prostate cancer (PCa) who have a component of BPH. Although medication can be effective, some patients need a procedure. Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is a principal surgical treatment for BPH with bladder outlet obstruction (BOO), but it can cause complications. PAE is a minimally invasive surgical therapy performed under local anaesthesia in an outpatient setting. It produces prostatic ischaemia followed by a reduction in prostate size. Prior short-term research reports an improvement of approximately 10 points on the International Prostate Symptom Score, but longer follow-up and comparisons with other minimally invasive surgical therapies are still needed to establish its place in international guidelines.
objectives: Assess complications, treatment effects, and reintervention after PAE in a nationwide Danish cohort.
Evaluate short-, mid-, and long-term clinical and procedural outcomes after PAE.
interpretation: The authors interpret PAE as providing sustained relief of LUTS with a favourable safety profile, including for patients with severe symptoms, catheter dependence or PCa. Catheter removal was achieved in 60% of initially catheter-dependent patients, and symptom improvement persisted at long-term assessment. A larger baseline PV was associated with greater symptom reduction but also a higher risk of PES. Sexual health scores improved after PAE. Surgical reintervention reached 18% (95% CI: 11–25%) at 5 yr; the authors suggest this may reflect an initially inadequate response rather than symptom recurrence. Unilateral embolisation was associated with more reintervention than bilateral embolisation, although the difference was not statistically significant.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors consider their short-term symptom and urinary-flow findings consistent with earlier PAE studies. Previous studies with <30 IUC-dependent patients reported catheter removal in 73–75%, whereas PAE studies with up to 73 IUC-dependent patients reported 66%; the authors regard their 60% rate as a more pragmatic estimate. In a cited TURP study of 10 654 men, 28% (2927 patients) had an IUC before surgery and 88% of that group achieved catheter removal, but morbidity and mortality were higher than among men without an IUC. A cited high-energy TUMT study reported 79% catheter removal at short term. The authors report a frequency of PAE-related AEs relative to patients of 70%, compared with 75% in a trial of PAE versus TURP; that trial reported approximately twice as many TURP-related AEs. Earlier PAE studies reported surgical reintervention rates of 10% to 20% at 2–3 yr, compared with 5.8% to 9.5% at 5 yr in cited TURP studies, 11% at 2–3 yr after PUL, and 7.3–10% at long-term follow-up after high-energy TUMT. A cited meta-analysis found no significant difference in reintervention between PAE and PUL, although PUL recipients had substantially smaller prostates.
clinical_implications: The findings support PAE as an option for symptom relief in patients with severe LUTS and large prostates, including those who are catheter dependent or have PCa.
The authors found few short-term complications and observed no long-term complications after PAE; PES was the most frequent AE and SAE.
For patients with larger baseline PV, the possibility of greater symptom improvement is accompanied by a higher risk of PES.
The need for surgical reintervention or continued medication remains relevant despite sustained symptom improvement.
practice_implications: The authors suggest favouring bilateral over unilateral embolisation to optimise success.
The authors suggest informing patients with larger baseline PV that they may experience greater efficacy but also face a higher risk of PES.
The authors state that fever-related hospitalisations linked to PES should be managed conservatively.
The authors consider PAE a treatment option for patients with severe LUTS and large prostates who choose a MIST, including patients with catheter dependence or PCa.
limitations: Insufficient follow-up limits the study’s internal validity, so its findings require cautious interpretation.
The absence of a comparison cohort treated with another MIST or TURP limits extrapolation to the general population.
Attrition could affect the questionnaire findings. The authors note that the 79% response rate reduced this concern.
Attrition might overestimate adverse long-term outcomes in the small longitudinal cohort, whose DAN-PSS was 22 points (IQR 8.5–32), compared with 9 points (IQR 3–21) in the cross-sectional study.
strengths: The authors describe their cohort as, to their knowledge, the largest to date of catheter-dependent patients undergoing PAE.
Including patients with PCa allowed the authors to assess treatment safety in that group.
The authors state that the questionnaire response rate of approximately 80% minimised potential attrition bias.
open_questions: How long-term PAE outcomes compare with those of other surgical procedures remains unresolved.
Which patients benefit most from PAE requires further clarification.
future_directions: Compare long-term PAE outcomes with those of other MISTs and surgical procedures.
Conduct further clinical trials to clarify which patients are most likely to benefit from PAE.
study_design: Nationwide, multicentre prospective cohort study using prospectively maintained health records and research databases, supplemented by a cross-sectional long-term questionnaire study.

population.description: Men in Denmark who underwent PAE for lower urinary tract symptoms between August 2017 and December 2022, including men with prostate cancer. The median age was 72 yr (IQR 66–76 yr); 88 (26%) patients used an IUC or ISC at the time of PAE.
inclusion_criteria: Underwent PAE for lower urinary tract symptoms in Denmark between August 2017 and December 2022; men with prostate cancer were eligible.
exclusion_criteria: PAE performed for macrohaematuria; 20 patients were excluded for this reason.
population.care_setting: PAE was performed as an outpatient procedure at Copenhagen University Hospital—Rigshospitalet or Odense University Hospital.

interventions: PAE under local anaesthesia, with an interventional radiologist embolising the prostatic arteries under fluoroscopic guidance; bilateral embolisation was intended.
An attempt to discontinue catheter use 4 wk after PAE in patients using an IUC.
comparators: Unilateral versus bilateral PAE for the analysis of surgical reintervention.
Catheter users versus noncatheter users for comparisons of adverse events.

primary: Adverse events possibly related to PAE and all serious adverse events during 90 d of follow-up; postembolisation syndrome and urinary retention were assessed separately.
Changes in symptoms measured with DAN-PSS, including short-, mid-, and long-term outcomes.
secondary: Prostate volume measured by transrectal ultrasound and urinary function assessed by uroflowmetry.

statistical_methods: Numerical variables were summarised as medians with IQRs, and categorical variables as counts with proportions. The chi-square test compared catheter users with noncatheter users. Univariable and multivariable linear regression assessed associations between baseline and follow-up prostate volume and DAN-PSS; the multivariable model adjusted for baseline prostate volume and DAN-PSS. Cause-specific cumulative incidence of retreatment was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen estimator, treating death as a competing risk. A Cox proportional hazard model compared reintervention risk after unilateral versus bilateral PAE. Statistical significance was defined as p <0.05. Analyses used R version 2024.04.2.
follow_up: Adverse events were assessed at 90 d. Standard care included an outpatient visit at 3 mo and health-record monitoring for a minimum of 1 yr. Outcomes were grouped as short term (0–6 mo), midterm (6 mo to 2 yr), and long term (above 2 yr). The cross-sectional questionnaires were completed between October 5, 2024, and December 27, 2024.

subgroup_analyses: At 2 yr, estimated cumulative surgical reintervention was 16% (95% CI: 5.2–27%) after unilateral PAE, compared with 8.5% (95% CI: 5.2–12%) after bilateral PAE.
The reported risk of reintervention was 43% (95% CI: –75% to 30%, p = 0.18) lower with bilateral than unilateral embolisation; the difference was not statistically significant.

Among patients using an IUC or ISC at the time of PAE, urinary tract infection was the only AE reported more often than in patients not using these catheters (p = 0.01). Apart from urinary tract infections, the discussion reports no significant AE differences between catheter users and catheter-free patients.

The discussion reports safety and efficacy after PAE among patients with severe LUTS or urinary retention, including patients with PCa, without providing a separate numerical effect estimate for the PCa subgroup.
secondary_results: Of 356 patients who underwent PAE during the study period, 20 were excluded because macrohaematuria was the indication; 336 were included in the analyses.

Before PAE, 188 (56%) patients had experienced urinary retention, while 88 (26%) were using an IUC or ISC at the intervention.
At baseline, 179 (53%) patients completed DAN-PSS; their median score was 30 points (IQR 23–44).

Table 1 reports CCI values of 0 in 142 (42%), 1 in 79 (24%), 2 in 55 (16%), and >2 in 60 (18%) of 336 patients. The median BMI was 26 (IQR 24–29) kg/m2 among 158 patients, and 42 (13%) of 336 had prostate cancer.

Among 251 patients with smoking-status data, 137 (55%) had never smoked, 95 (38%) were ex-smokers, and 19 (7.6%) were active smokers; median exposure among ex-smokers and active smokers was 25 (IQR 10–35) pack years.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that PAE provides sustained relief of LUTS with a favourable adverse-event profile, although some patients need further treatment or continued medication. They regard it as an option for patients with severe LUTS and large prostates seeking a MIST, including patients with catheter dependency or PCa.
narrative_summary:
This nationwide, multicentre prospective cohort assessed complications, symptom outcomes and retreatment after PAE for LUTS in Denmark. The analysis included 336 patients treated between August 2017 and December 2022, including men with PCa. Median age was 72 yr (IQR 66–76 yr), and 88 (26%) used IUC or ISC at the time of treatment. Outcomes came from clinical follow-up and a later cross-sectional questionnaire study.

Within 90 d, 26 patients (7.7%) experienced a serious adverse event, while postembolisation syndrome occurred in 132 (39%). Among the 88 initially catheter-dependent men, 53 (60%) were catheter free at 0–6 mo. The median DAN-PSS was 6 points (IQR 1–16) at 0–6 mo and 9 points (IQR 3–21) at >2 yr. Estimated surgical reintervention reached 9.5% (95% CI: 6.3–13%) at 2 yr and 18% (95% CI: 11–25%) at 5 yr; medical retreatment was also reported.

The cross-sectional questionnaire response rate was 79% (250/314), with median follow-up of 3.4 yr (IQR 2.7–4.1 yr). The authors interpret these findings as supporting PAE for selected patients with severe symptoms, large prostates or catheter dependency, while stressing that insufficient follow-up and the absence of a control cohort limit interpretation. They call for comparisons with other surgical treatments to clarify PAE’s long-term place in BPH care.

document_sections.heading: Background and objective:
document_sections.content: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) can substantially reduce men's quality of life. Prostatic artery embolisation (PAE) is described as a safe and effective treatment for LUTS. The study assessed complications, treatment outcomes, and subsequent intervention after PAE.

document_sections.heading: Methods:
document_sections.content: This multicentre prospective cohort included patients treated with PAE from 2017 to 2022 and used cross-sectional questionnaires for long-term assessment. An interventional radiologist performed outpatient PAE under local anaesthesia, using fluoroscopy to guide embolisation; the resulting ischaemia leads to a reduction in prostate size. Adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) were assessed 90 d after PAE. Outcomes were assessed with the Danish Prostate Symptom Score (DAN-PSS), transrectal ultrasound, uroflowmetry, and cessation of catheter use. Retreatment was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen estimator.

document_sections.heading: Key findings and limitations:
document_sections.content: The cohort comprised 336 patients. Median age was 72 yr (interquartile range [IQR] 66–76 yr), and median prostate volume was 101 cm3 (IQR 81–147 cm3). At baseline, 88 (26%) depended on a catheter; among the remaining patients, median DAN-PSS was 30 points (IQR 23–44). An SAE affected 26 (7.7%) patients, postembolisation syndrome affected 132 (39%), and another minor AE affected 106 (32%). At 0–6 mo, median DAN-PSS was 6 points (IQR 1–16), and 53/88 (60%) initially catheter-dependent patients no longer needed a catheter. At >2 yr, median DAN-PSS was 9 points (IQR 3–21). Reintervention rates were 9.5% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 6.3–13%) at 2 yr and 18% (95% CI: 11–25%) at 5 yr. The questionnaire response rate was 79%. Limitations were inadequate follow-up data and the absence of a control cohort.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions and clinical implications:
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that PAE provided safe, effective, and durable treatment for selected patients in Denmark with severe LUTS, catheter dependency, and large prostates. During 5-yr follow-up, 18% needed retreatment; the authors state that this should be considered in light of the patients' initially restricted treatment options.

document_sections.heading: What does this study add?
document_sections.content: The study adds information on complications, outcomes, and reintervention after PAE. The authors report few complications, generally minor ones, and an overall improvement in sexual health score. They describe this as, to their knowledge, the largest PAE cohort of catheter-dependent patients to date and consider its findings supportive of safety and efficacy in that group. Inclusion of patients with prostate cancer also provides safety information for those patients. Cross-sectional long-term data suggest that mild symptom scores persist for >3 yr after PAE. The authors emphasise that comparison with other surgical procedures is needed to establish PAE's place in benign prostatic hyperplasia treatment.

document_sections.heading: Patient Summary
document_sections.content: The study examined PAE for urinary problems associated with benign prostate enlargement. The authors found it safe and effective and report that patients with severe symptoms or urinary retention maintained a mild symptom score >3 yr after treatment. They call for further clinical trials to clarify which patients benefit most.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: LUTS can markedly impair quality of life and occur in at least 30% of men older than 65 yr. They commonly accompany benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), but can also occur in men with prostate cancer (PCa) who have a BPH component. Medication is effective, although surgery may be needed. Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) remains the principal surgical treatment for BPH with bladder outlet obstruction (BOO), but can cause urethral strictures, incontinence, sepsis, bleeding, and retrograde ejaculation. Population ageing, comorbidity, and polypharmacy increase demand for lower-risk procedures that avoid general anaesthesia and reduce complications. Minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs) seek to preserve clinical benefit while reducing the morbidity of BPH surgery. PAE is an outpatient MIST performed under local anaesthesia. Fluoroscopically guided embolisation of the prostatic arteries causes tissue ischaemia followed by gradual shrinkage. The article describes PAE as safe and effective for BPH-related LUTS, with lower prostate volume (PV) and significant clinical improvement. Prior short-term findings indicate an approximately 10-point reduction in severe LUTS on the International Prostate Symptom Score. Longer follow-up and comparisons with other MISTs remain necessary for acceptance under international guidelines. Using prospectively maintained records and questionnaires, the authors aimed to assess short-, mid-, and long-term clinical and procedural outcomes in a nationwide Danish cohort following the introduction of PAE in 2017.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Study design and population
document_sections.content: The multicentre study included all patients in Denmark treated with PAE for LUTS between August 2017 and December 2022, including men with PCa. Data came from prospectively maintained electronic records and research databases. The two treatment institutions were Copenhagen University HospitalRigshospitalet and Odense University Hospital. The procedure was intended to be bilateral. Study approvals were R–23002071 and P2023-52. Potentially PAE-related AEs and all SAEs were evaluated at 90 d. An SAE was an event or reaction, whether or not procedure-related, that caused death, threatened life, required or prolonged hospitalisation, or produced persistent or substantial disability or incapacity. Postembolisation syndrome (PES) was assessed separately and comprised dysuria, urgency, frequent urination, worsening LUTS, pelvic or prostatic pain, nausea, or fever, alone or together, within the first 7 d after PAE. Urinary retention was recorded separately. Routine care included an outpatient assessment at 3 mo and record-based monitoring for at least 1 yr. The 3-mo assessment used the DAN-PSS, transrectal ultrasound for PV, and uroflowmetry. Patients dependent on a urinary catheter did not receive the DAN-PSS. This validated Danish patient-reported measure has 12 questions on storage and voiding function and related quality-of-life effects. Scores of <8 points indicate mild symptoms, 8–19 points moderate symptoms, and >19 points severe symptoms. Its three sexual-health questions form the Danish Prostate Symptom Score Sexual Score [DAN-PSSsex], used to compare erectile and ejaculatory function and associated bother before and after treatment. Cessation of catheter use was attempted 4 wk after PAE in indwelling urinary catheter (IUC) users. Outcome periods were defined as 0–6 mo for short term, 6 mo to 2 yr for midterm, and above 2 yr for long term. Subjective symptoms came from the DAN-PSS; severe LUTS also included IUC or clean intermittent self-catheterisation (ISC) users. For long-term evaluation, patients completed electronic questionnaires on patient-reported outcomes, including DAN-PSS and retreatment, between October 5, 2024, and December 27, 2024.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Statistical analysis
document_sections.content: Numerical variables were summarised as medians and IQRs, and categorical variables as counts and proportions. The chi-square test compared catheter users with nonusers. Univariable and multivariable linear regression assessed associations between baseline and follow-up PV and DAN-PSS; multivariable models adjusted for baseline PV and DAN-PSS. Cause-specific cumulative retreatment incidence was estimated from PAE to an event or the end of follow-up with the Aalen-Johansen estimator, treating death as a competing risk. A Cox proportional hazard model compared reintervention risk after unilateral versus bilateral PAE until an event, death, or the end of follow-up. Statistical significance was defined as p <0.05. Analyses used R version 2024.04.2.

document_sections.heading: 3. Results
document_sections.content: During the study period, 356 patients underwent PAE; 20 were excluded because their indication was macrohaematuria, leaving 336 for analysis. Median age was 72 yr (IQR 66–76 yr); 60 (18%) had a Charlson Comorbidity Index of >2, and 114 (45%) were current or former smokers. Before PAE, 188 (56%) had experienced urinary retention, and 88 (26%) used an IUC or ISC at intervention. At baseline, 179 (53%) completed the DAN-PSS, with a median of 30 points (IQR 23–44). Table 1 presents baseline characteristics and procedural details. Overall, 234 AEs were reported in 176 patients (53%), and 27 SAEs in 26 patients (7.7%). Every SAE involved hospitalisation or an extension of an existing admission; 22 (85%) of the affected patients were discharged within a week. PES affected 132 (39%) and lasted a median of 8 d (IQR 4–14 d). For every 10 cm3 greater baseline PV, PES risk rose by 4% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0–9%, p = 0.04), and PES duration increased by 0.6 d (95% CI: 0.1–1.1 d, p = 0.02). Urinary tract infection was the only AE more frequent among patients using an IUC or ISC at intervention (p = 0.01). Table 2 lists AEs and SAEs within 90 d after PAE, alongside hospitalisation durations; patients could have more than one event. Among the 88 baseline IUC or ISC users, 53 (60%) were catheter free at 0–6 mo. At that interval, median DAN-PSS was 6 points (IQR 1–16). The figures present longitudinal DAN-PSS, maximum flow rate (Qmax), postvoid residual urine volume, and PV, as well as symptom-severity categories. In the efficacy figure, mild corresponds to 0–7, moderate to 8–19, and severe to >19; absence of LUTS without further urological intervention is classified as mild, whereas catheterisation is classified as severe LUTS. After adjustment for baseline DAN-PSS, every 10 cm3 higher PV was associated with a 0.66-point decrease in DAN-PSS (95% CI: 0.22–1.1, p = 0.004). For each 1-point higher baseline DAN-PSS, short-term DAN-PSS was 0.05 points higher (95% CI: –0.09 to 0.2, p = 0.49). Cumulative surgical reintervention was 9.5% (95% CI: 6.3–13%) at 2 yr and 18% (95% CI: 11–25%) at 5 yr. Cumulative medical retreatment was 14% (95% CI: 11–18%) at 2 yr and 30% (95% CI: 18–42%) at 5 yr. At 2 yr, cumulative surgical reintervention was 16% (95% CI: 5.2–27%) after unilateral PAE versus 8.5% (95% CI: 5.2–12%) after bilateral PAE. Bilateral embolisation was associated with a 43% (95% CI: –75% to 30%, p = 0.18) lower reintervention risk. Among men alive for the cross-sectional study, response was 79% (250/314), and median follow-up was 3.4 yr (IQR 2.7–4.1 yr). At that assessment, 14 (5.6%) used an IUC and 13 (5.2%) used ISC. Catheter-free men had a median DAN-PSS of 9 points (IQR 3–21). No sexual activity was reported by 11%; among sexually active patients, median DAN-PSSsex was 2.0 points (IQR 0.2–6.0). Of 224 respondents to the retreatment question, 21 (9.4%) reported surgical reintervention and 56 (25%) medical retreatment. A figure depicts surgical and medical retreatment over time.

document_sections.heading: 4. Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors sought to clarify immediate and longer-term effects of PAE. They note that its role as a MIST for BOO in BPH remains disputed because randomised comparisons against other MISTs are lacking. They interpret their findings as consistent with earlier evidence of safety and efficacy, including in severe LUTS or urinary retention, while acknowledging relatively high retreatment rates and the need for direct comparison with other procedures. Success in treating BOO depends partly on initial symptom severity and comorbidities, and patients often prioritise low short- and long-term complication risks. Short-term complications in this study were minor; PES was the most frequent AE and SAE. Hospitalisations were often fever-related, an association known for PES, and the authors state that these episodes should receive conservative treatment. If PES is regarded as an expected side effect, as Moreira et al suggest, procedure-related AEs affected only 32% (106/336). Consistent with earlier research, nontarget embolisation was uncommon, with three self-limited cases of penile ulceration. All AEs and SAEs resolved rapidly, and no long-term complications were observed. The authors report a frequency of PAE-related AEs relative to enrolled patients of 70%, compared with 75% in a cited randomised PAE-versus-TURP trial; that trial reported approximately twice as many TURP-related AEs. Apart from urinary tract infections, which were strongly associated with IUC use, AE rates did not differ significantly between catheter users and catheter-free patients. A cited large TURP study found significantly greater postoperative morbidity among IUC users. The authors therefore consider PAE potentially suitable for catheter-dependent patients and interpret its safety profile as favourable even with PCa or catheter dependence. Efficacy can mean either a mild symptom score or remaining catheter free. Over 25% of this cohort depended on a catheter, most were above 65 yr, and prostates were large; nevertheless, catheter removal succeeded in 60%. Many BPH surgery studies exclude catheter-dependent patients. Prior PAE studies with <30 IUC-dependent participants reported catheter removal in 73–75%, whereas studies including up to 73 such patients reported 66%; the authors suggest around 60% may be a more realistic rate. Catheter-dependent patients are also often regarded as poor candidates for resective surgery. In a cited TURP study of 10 654 men, 28% (2927 patients) used an IUC preoperatively and 88% achieved removal, but morbidity and mortality were higher in those with a preoperative IUC. For high-energy transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), another locally anaesthetised MIST available for larger prostates, a cited short-term catheter-removal rate was 79%. This study's short-term results resembled earlier PAE findings: 72% (162/225) had mild symptoms, and Qmax and postvoid residual urine volume improved. A cited systematic review of randomised TUMT trials reported a short-term decline in pooled mean symptom score from 19 points (severe) to 6.7 points (mild). The authors' data support a larger baseline PV as a predictor of greater subjective symptom improvement after PAE, but also of increased PES risk. Sexual function improved: median DAN-PSSsex was 3 points (IQR 0–6) at baseline and 2 points (IQR 0–6) at long-term follow-up. The authors suggest improved LUTS and freedom from catheter use as possible explanations. In contrast, a cited TURP study of 1014 patients did not find comparable improvement and reported an increase in total sexual-health score. The authors suggest informing patients with larger baseline PV that efficacy might be greater but PES risk might also rise. They interpret sustained long-term DAN-PSS improvement as evidence of durability. Attrition bias might overstate negative outcomes in their small longitudinal long-term cohort, whose DAN-PSS was 22 points (IQR 8.5–32), versus 9 points (IQR 3–21) in the cross-sectional study. Cross-sectional surgical reintervention was 9.4% at median follow-up of 3.4 yr (IQR 2.7–4.1 yr). Their estimated 5-yr cohort reintervention rate of 18% (95% CI: 11–25%) supports, but does not establish, the possibility that retreatment reflects an initially inadequate response rather than symptom recurrence. As in high-volume centres, 13% underwent unilateral PAE. Its reintervention rate was markedly higher than after bilateral PAE, although the difference was not statistically significant. Cited studies report surgical reintervention after PAE ranging from 10% to 20% at 2–3 yr; estimates vary, and retrospective studies may underestimate it. Large TURP studies report 5-yr rates of 5.8% to 9.5%. After prostatic urethral lift (PUL), cited rates are 11% at 2–3 yr. A recent meta-analysis found no significant PAE-versus-PUL reintervention difference, but PUL recipients had substantially smaller PVs. Cited long-term rates after high-energy TUMT were 7.3–10%. The authors consider PAE reintervention broadly comparable to other MISTs and suggest preferring bilateral embolisation to optimise success. They identify insufficient follow-up as a limitation of internal validity and urge corresponding caution in interpretation. Without a comparison cohort receiving other MISTs or TURP, generalisability is reduced. Attrition could weaken questionnaire findings, although the approximately 80% response rate may have reduced that bias.

document_sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that PAE provides safe, effective, and durable relief of LUTS with a favourable AE profile, despite variation in reintervention and the continued need for medication in some patients. They consider it a valid MIST option for patients with severe LUTS and large prostates, including those dependent on a catheter or with PCa.
